new_slides.title: Pacing can arise when searching never reaches its goal
body: Motivated behavior has two phases: an **appetitive phase** of searching, patrolling and travel, and a consummatory phase such as eating. Provided food satisfies the second phase without the first, so the drive to travel can remain active in an animal that is well fed.

When a motivated sequence is repeatedly started and blocked, the same movements tend to be repeated along the few routes the space allows. Greco and colleagues describe this frustration of highly motivated behavior as a cause of stereotypy, and propose that prolonged restriction may also change cortical and basal ganglia circuits so that repetition becomes harder to stop.

These two explanations predict different things. Pacing driven by present frustration should fall when the missing opportunity is supplied, whereas pacing that reflects altered circuits may persist after conditions improve, which is one reason past transfers can predict current stereotypy.

figure.caption: Clubb & Mason (2003), Fig. 1(a–b). Natural home range, infant mortality and pacing across carnivores.

transcript: Slides 3 and 5 connect pacing to wide natural ranging, and slides 42 and 43 connect elephant stereotypy to housing and life history; the motivational account of stereotypy links these findings.
Food satisfies only part of a foraging sequence.
Ethologists divide motivated behavior into a searching phase and a completing phase, and the searching phase has its own motivation.
Glaeser and colleagues cite the view that elephant walking is largely appetitive, a means of reaching food, companions and other resources, rather than travel performed for its own sake.
Blocked sequences become fixed routes.
Greco and colleagues argue that environments lacking variability, complexity or novelty frustrate highly motivated behaviors and can produce prolonged negative states.

A carnivore whose ranging is never completed by finding anything new repeats the start of the sequence, and in a bounded enclosure that repetition takes the form of the same path traced again and again.
Present frustration and lasting change are separate possibilities.
The same authors raise the possibility that such environments alter processing in cortical and basal ganglia systems in a way that promotes stereotypy.
If that happens, removing the original restriction may not remove the behavior, which fits the observation on slide 43 that a history of transfers predicts stereotypy in the present.
refs: Clubb R, Mason G (2003). Captivity effects on wide-ranging carnivores. Nature 425: 473-474. https://doi.org/10.1038/425473a

Greco BJ, Meehan CL, Hogan JN, Leighty KA, Mellen J, Mason GJ, Mench JA (2016). The Days and Nights of Zoo Elephants: Using Epidemiology to Better Understand Stereotypic Behavior of African Elephants (Loxodonta africana) and Asian Elephants (Elephas maximus) in North American Zoos. PLOS ONE 11: e0144276. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0144276

Glaeser SS, Shepherdson D, Lewis K, Prado N, Brown JL, Lee B, Wielebnowski N (2021). Supporting Zoo Asian Elephant (Elephas maximus) Welfare and Herd Dynamics with a More Complex and Expanded Habitat. Animals 11: 2566. https://doi.org/10.3390/ani11092566

new_slides.title: A looming visitor resembles an attacking predator
body: Little penguins are hunted by land, aerial and aquatic predators, so a large shape that rises above them and moves suddenly matches the cues of an attack. Chiew and colleagues identify leaning over the pool edge, the most frequent visitor action, as the probable trigger, since it resembles an aerial predator descending on prey.

Defensive responses trade other activities for safety. A vigilant bird spends time scanning instead of preening, and a huddling or retreating bird gives up surface swimming, which the authors regard as a highly motivated behavior in a species that spends most of its wild day foraging at sea.

**Habituation**, a decline in response to a repeated stimulus that has no consequence, did not erase these responses. Visitor contact at the pool edge was intense and unpredictable, conditions under which a defensive response tends to persist rather than fade.

figure.caption: Chiew et al. (2019), Fig. 4(a–d). Penguins and the habitat areas sampled by the cameras.

new_slides.cite: Chiew et al. (2019); Chiew et al. (2020)
transcript: Slides 7 to 9 record which visitor actions the barrier removed and how penguin behavior changed; the penguin's predator ecology explains why those particular actions matter.
Visitor actions overlap with predator cues.
Chiew and colleagues list foxes, cats, water rats, sea eagles, large gulls and fur seals among the predators of little penguins, the smallest penguin species.
They cite work in which a person standing low on the horizon disturbed nesting penguins less than a person looming over them, which points to the vertical approach as the threatening feature.
Fear has a cost in lost behavior.
Comfort behaviors such as preening are generally performed when an animal is not threatened, so their return near the covered window on slide 11 is evidence of reduced threat.
Swimming persisted even though food was provided on land, which the authors take as evidence that it is highly motivated, so its suppression by close visitors is a welfare cost in itself.
Habituation depends on what the stimulus predicts.
Some wild penguins habituate to people, depending on their experience and the amount of exposure.

Close contact at the zoo pool edge included banging, splashing and sudden movement, varied from moment to moment and was never paired with anything rewarding, which the authors suggest keeps it fear-provoking.
refs: Chiew SJ, Butler KL, Sherwen SL, Coleman GJ, Fanson KV, Hemsworth PH (2019). Effects of Regulating Visitor Viewing Proximity and the Intensity of Visitor Behaviour on Little Penguin (Eudyptula minor) Behaviour and Welfare. Animals 9: 285. https://doi.org/10.3390/ani9060285

Chiew SJ, Butler KL, Sherwen SL, Coleman GJ, Melfi V, Burns A, Hemsworth PH (2020). Effect of Covering a Visitor Viewing Area Window on the Behaviour of Zoo-Housed Little Penguins (Eudyptula minor). Animals 10: 1224. https://doi.org/10.3390/ani10071224

new_slides.title: Fecal hormones lag behavior by hours and average many events
body: The **HPA axis** links the hypothalamus, pituitary and adrenal cortex: a perceived threat triggers hypothalamic and pituitary signals that make the adrenal cortex secrete glucocorticoids, corticosterone in birds. The liver metabolizes the hormone, and the metabolites appear in feces after a delay.

In this penguin colony the median delay from a stressor to the fecal response was 7 hours, so samples collected late in the afternoon reflected the morning's events mixed with everything else that day. Pooled samples from unidentified birds averaged across individuals as well as across time.

Chiew and colleagues offer two explanations for the unchanged hormone measure. Retreat and vigilance may have removed each bird from the threat quickly enough to limit adrenal activation, or the one- to two-day treatments were too short to shift a measure that integrates over hours.

figure.caption: Chiew et al. (2019), Fig. 2. The physical barrier that increased visitor viewing distance.

new_slides.cite: Chiew et al. (2019); Chiew et al. (2020)
transcript: Slide 10 contrasts changed behavior with unchanged fecal glucocorticoid metabolites; the physiology of the measure and the sampling design explain how both can be true.
Two stress systems respond on different timescales.
Chiew and colleagues describe the sympatho-adrenal medullary system, which releases catecholamines within seconds, and the HPA axis, which releases glucocorticoids more slowly.
A fecal assay samples only the second system, and only after the hormone has been metabolized and excreted.
Timing and pooling shape what the assay can detect.
Earlier work on this population found a median excretion lag of 7 hours, with a peak on average 10.8 hours after a health check, so the authors collected samples at the end of each treatment day.
Individual birds often could not be identified, so a strong response in a few penguins could be diluted by samples from birds that stayed away from the visitors.
Avoidance can be a successful coping response.
The authors propose that moving away from the visitor edge may have reduced the stress response itself, which would make the behavioral change the reason the hormone did not rise.
The corner retreat on slide 12 offers exactly this kind of option, and the elephant hormone records on slide 28 face the same timing questions over a much longer study.
refs: Chiew SJ, Butler KL, Sherwen SL, Coleman GJ, Fanson KV, Hemsworth PH (2019). Effects of Regulating Visitor Viewing Proximity and the Intensity of Visitor Behaviour on Little Penguin (Eudyptula minor) Behaviour and Welfare. Animals 9: 285. https://doi.org/10.3390/ani9060285

Chiew SJ, Butler KL, Sherwen SL, Coleman GJ, Melfi V, Burns A, Hemsworth PH (2020). Effect of Covering a Visitor Viewing Area Window on the Behaviour of Zoo-Housed Little Penguins (Eudyptula minor). Animals 10: 1224. https://doi.org/10.3390/ani10071224

new_slides.title: Covering a window removed sound and vibration as well as sight
body: Chiew and colleagues assigned the covered and uncovered treatments to days at random and ran them only on school-working days. Random assignment spreads weather, keeper routines and other daily variation evenly across treatments, and avoiding weekends removed the systematic surge in visitors that would otherwise accompany some days and not others.

The barrier went up the afternoon before each covered day, giving the penguins time to adjust to its appearance, so a response on the treatment day reflects the absence of visitors at the window rather than the novelty of the cover.

What the design cannot separate is the channel of the threat. The cover blocked vision, but it also kept visitors from banging on the glass and moving suddenly near it, and sound and vibration travel well through water. Each channel could have driven the penguins' avoidance.

figure.caption: Chiew et al. (2020), Fig. 2(a–b). Glass viewing windows and the visitor pathway.

transcript: Slides 11 to 13 describe what changed when one window was covered; the design explains which alternative explanations the experiment removes and which it leaves open.
Random day assignment removes day-to-day confounds.
Each treatment was imposed for single days, with five replicates of each over two weeks, in an order set at random.
Running only on school-working days avoided the normal swings in attendance on weekends and holidays, which would otherwise have been confused with the treatment.
An acclimation period separates novelty from treatment.
A new object in an enclosure can provoke avoidance on its own, so installing the barrier the previous afternoon reduced this possibility.
Keeping the timing of observations clear of the close-up feeding encounter likewise kept a predictable daily event from mixing with the treatment.
The channel of threat remains open.
Chiew and colleagues point out that little penguins hunt by vision and see well, but also that water carries sound faster and with less loss than air.
The signage result on slide 9 adds a parallel: when an intervention changes several visitor actions at once, the penguin data alone cannot assign the effect to one of them.
refs: Chiew SJ, Butler KL, Sherwen SL, Coleman GJ, Melfi V, Burns A, Hemsworth PH (2020). Effect of Covering a Visitor Viewing Area Window on the Behaviour of Zoo-Housed Little Penguins (Eudyptula minor). Animals 10: 1224. https://doi.org/10.3390/ani10071224

extra_figures.caption: Chiew et al. (2020), Fig. 3. The opaque barrier used in the window-covering experiment.

new_slides.title: Double labeling ties activity to a defined pathway
body: Neural activity raises intracellular calcium, which switches on transcription of the **immediate early gene** _c-fos_; the Fos protein then accumulates in the nucleus over the following hour or two. Baratta and colleagues perfused the rats 2 hours after the last shock to catch this window, so a Fos-labeled nucleus marks a cell that was strongly driven during the session.

Tracer deposits vary in size, which changes how many prefrontal cells become labeled. Expressing results as the percentage of tracer-labeled cells that also contained Fos, and checking that labeled-cell counts did not differ between groups, keeps deposit size from masquerading as a treatment effect.

Fos has limits. It marks strong excitation but not inhibition, and its absence does not prove a cell was silent. The double label therefore identifies which projection cells control recruited, not what they did at their targets.

figure.caption: Baratta et al. (2009), Fig. 2(A–C). Prefrontal activation following controllable or uncontrollable stress.

transcript: Slides 15 and 16 combine a retrograde tracer with Fos staining; the biology of Fos and the controls built into the counts explain what the double label can and cannot establish.
Fos is a delayed readout of strong activity.
Activity-driven calcium entry activates transcription of c-fos, and the protein product builds up in the nucleus over hours, where an antibody can detect it.
Baratta and colleagues processed tissue 2 hours after the final shock in both experiments, so the stain captured activity during the stress session itself.
The counts were designed to defeat tracer variability.
Only rats whose fluorogold deposit stayed within the dorsal raphe were analyzed, so labeled prefrontal cells were genuinely raphe-projecting.
The number of tracer-labeled cells did not differ between groups and was entered as a covariate, which rules out larger deposits as the reason one group showed more double-labeled cells.
Total Fos and projection Fos answer different questions.
Escapable and inescapable shock produced the same total Fos in prelimbic cortex, so a whole-region count would have suggested that control made no difference.
The authors emphasize that total Fos alone can be an insufficient measure at the systems level, which is why identifying the target of each activated cell was decisive.
refs: Baratta MV, Zarza CM, Gomez DM, Campeau S, Watkins LR, Maier SF (2009). Selective activation of dorsal raphe nucleus‐projecting neurons in the ventral medial prefrontal cortex by controllable stress. European Journal of Neuroscience 30: 1111-1116. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1460-9568.2009.06867.x

extra_figures.caption: Baratta et al. (2009), Fig. 1(A–B). Dorsal raphe tracer deposit and labeled prefrontal neurons.

new_slides.title: Uncontrollable stress sensitizes serotonin neurons for days
body: Inescapable shock activates dorsal raphe serotonin neurons more than escapable shock does, and this activation leaves them **sensitized**: for a period afterward, ordinary inputs make them release exaggerated amounts of serotonin in their target regions. Baratta and colleagues describe this excess release as the proximate cause of the exaggerated fear and reduced social exploration that follow uncontrollable stress.
Control works upstream. Prelimbic cells that detect a successful escape inhibit the raphe through local GABA cells, so the raphe never reaches the sensitized state.

Inactivation experiments make this necessity explicit. Silencing ventral medial prefrontal cortex with the GABA agonist muscimol during escapable shock made controllable stress produce the same serotonin and behavioral outcomes as uncontrollable stress, even though the rat still turned the wheel.

figure.caption: Baratta et al. (2009), Fig. 3(A–C). Prefrontal activation after prior experience with stressor control.

transcript: Slides 14 to 17 identify a prefrontal projection that responds to control and propose how it inhibits the raphe; the consequences of raphe activation explain why that inhibition matters for behavior.
Sensitization converts one session into a lasting vulnerability.
In the introduction to their paper, Baratta and colleagues explain that inescapable shock activates raphe serotonin neurons more strongly than escapable shock does.
The result is a period during which inputs to the raphe release exaggerated serotonin in projection regions, and the behavioral effects of uncontrollable stress depend on this release.
The raphe does not compute controllability.
The authors argue that the raphe responds to the shock itself, while the ventral medial prefrontal cortex detects whether the animal's actions are working.
This division of labor explains why the selective recruitment of raphe-projecting prelimbic cells on slide 16 is the expected signature of control.
Inactivation tests necessity.
When muscimol silenced the prefrontal region during escapable shock, control no longer protected the rat, so prefrontal activity is necessary for the buffering effect.
The same inactivation at the time of the first experience prevented the later protection shown on slide 18, linking the two experiments to one pathway.
refs: Baratta MV, Zarza CM, Gomez DM, Campeau S, Watkins LR, Maier SF (2009). Selective activation of dorsal raphe nucleus‐projecting neurons in the ventral medial prefrontal cortex by controllable stress. European Journal of Neuroscience 30: 1111-1116. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1460-9568.2009.06867.x

new_slides.title: Retreats and partner choice give zoo animals a form of control
body: In the rat experiments, control means that the animal's own action changes an aversive event. Zoo habitats offer a comparable contingency when an animal can move away from a stimulus or toward a companion: the penguin corner hidden from visitors and the Oregon elephants' choice of social partners both make exposure depend on the animal's behavior.

This parallel is a hypothesis, not an established mechanism in penguins or elephants. Neither zoo study recorded prefrontal or raphe activity, so the rat circuit supplies a reason to expect control to matter rather than evidence that it operates the same way in these species.

If the parallel holds, a retreat would protect even on days it goes unused, since the availability of escape is the variable the rat experiments manipulated, separately from the amount of stimulation received.

figure.caption: Chiew et al. (2020), Fig. 1. The penguin encounter habitat and viewing areas.

new_slides.cite: Baratta et al. (2009); Chiew et al. (2020); Glaeser et al. (2021)
transcript: Slides 14 to 18 establish that control over a stressor changes its neural impact in rats; slides 12, 31 and 32 describe zoo habitats that give animals choices about exposure and companions.
Control is a contingency between action and outcome.
Yoking on slide 14 held the shocks constant and changed only whether the rat's behavior ended them.
A penguin swimming into a corner that visitors cannot see changes its own exposure in the same way, and Chiew and colleagues suggest that such a refuge may reduce the welfare risk of visitor contact.
Species and preparation must stay identifiable.
The neural findings come from rats receiving tail shock, and no comparable recording exists for the zoo animals in this deck.
The rat work therefore justifies measuring choice as a welfare variable, while whether choice protects these species has to be tested in them.
Availability can matter apart from use.
In the immunization experiment, an earlier experience of control changed the response to later stress that the rat could not control.
Glaeser and colleagues describe the Oregon habitat as giving elephants more autonomy over where to be and with whom, which is the zoo counterpart of making control available.
refs: Baratta MV, Zarza CM, Gomez DM, Campeau S, Watkins LR, Maier SF (2009). Selective activation of dorsal raphe nucleus‐projecting neurons in the ventral medial prefrontal cortex by controllable stress. European Journal of Neuroscience 30: 1111-1116. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1460-9568.2009.06867.x

Chiew SJ, Butler KL, Sherwen SL, Coleman GJ, Melfi V, Burns A, Hemsworth PH (2020). Effect of Covering a Visitor Viewing Area Window on the Behaviour of Zoo-Housed Little Penguins (Eudyptula minor). Animals 10: 1224. https://doi.org/10.3390/ani10071224

Glaeser SS, Shepherdson D, Lewis K, Prado N, Brown JL, Lee B, Wielebnowski N (2021). Supporting Zoo Asian Elephant (Elephas maximus) Welfare and Herd Dynamics with a More Complex and Expanded Habitat. Animals 11: 2566. https://doi.org/10.3390/ani11092566

extra_figures.caption: Chiew et al. (2020), Fig. 6(a–b). Penguin visibility across habitat areas with the window uncovered and covered.

new_slides.title: Kinship stabilizes elephant groups by keeping ranks settled
body: Wild Asian and African elephants live in matrilineal groups: adult females stay with mothers, sisters and daughters for life, and when groups split, first-degree relatives remain together. Captive groups assembled from unrelated females lack this shared history.

Relatedness can lower conflict through two routes. Helping relatives benefits genes they share, an evolutionary reason for tolerance, while relatives raised together have also had years to settle their ranks. A **dominance hierarchy** may be established by fights but is maintained when the lower-ranking animal consistently yields, so a settled group needs little aggression.

Harvey and colleagues' less-related group suggests what happens without settled ranks: one elephant's behavior toward another shifted from mostly affiliative in spring to mostly agonistic in autumn, a relationship that had not stabilized.

figure.caption: Harvey et al. (2018), Fig. 5(a–b). Directed affiliative relationships among individual elephants.

transcript: Slides 19 to 23 compare a related and a less-related elephant group; the natural social structure of elephants and the logic of dominance explain why relatedness changes the balance of affiliation and conflict.
Wild society is built on female kin.
Harvey and colleagues report that no study of wild Asian elephants has found adult females transferring between groups, so females remain in their natal groupings.
Groups are led by an older female who serves as a source of social knowledge, and allomothering, help with a calf from a female other than its mother, is common.
Evolutionary and developmental explanations differ.
The evolutionary reason is that tolerance and help directed at relatives promote copies of shared genes.

The developmental reason is that relatives in a zoo group have usually lived together since birth, so familiarity and settled ranks may explain the same pattern; the two-group comparison cannot separate these routes.
Unsettled relationships produce shifting conflict.
In the less-related group, one female directed 32 affiliative and 17 agonistic acts toward another in spring, but 10 affiliative and 28 agonistic acts in autumn.
The authors interpret the frequent non-contact displacement on slide 22 as evidence of a functional hierarchy in the related group that the less-related group lacked.
refs: Harvey ND, Daly C, Clark N, Ransford E, Wallace S, Yon L (2018). Social Interactions in Two Groups of Zoo-Housed Adult Female Asian Elephants (Elephas maximus) that Differ in Relatedness. Animals 8: 132. https://doi.org/10.3390/ani8080132

new_slides.title: GPS distance must be cleaned to measure purposeful travel
body: The Oregon GPS bracelets recorded a position every 5 seconds, and distance was summed from successive fixes. Satellite signals are blocked inside buildings, so fixes taken while elephants were indoors were removed, which makes the measure an outdoor distance by design.

A distance also counts every step, including repetitive route tracing. When Glaeser and colleagues subtracted time spent in repetitive behavior, one female's walking still roughly doubled between habitats, from 7.3 to 14.7 km per day, so the increase reflected purposeful travel rather than more pacing.

The mother of the calf was not fitted with a bracelet, since her movement was expected to follow her calf's. Choices like these determine which question a distance answers: how far an elephant chooses to travel when its own needs set the route.

figure.caption: Glaeser et al. (2021), Fig. 4(c–d). An elephant’s GPS locations in warm and cool seasons.

transcript: Slides 25 and 27 report walking distance and space use from GPS records; the way those records were processed decides whether a longer distance means richer behavior or simply more pacing.
Sampling rate and signal loss shape the number.
Fixes every 5 seconds capture detailed paths, but each fix carries some location error and the receiver loses the satellites indoors.
Removing indoor points means the reported distances describe outdoor movement only, and Holdgate and colleagues likewise reported outdoor distances in their multi-zoo study.
Pacing inflates distance.
Slides 3 and 5 separate repetitive route tracing from flexible locomotion, and a GPS track cannot tell them apart on its own.
Combining the GPS data with behavioral observation allowed the authors to remove repetitive behavior and confirm that both tracked females still walked farther in the new habitat.
Who is measured defines the question.
A mother accompanying a young calf moves at the calf's pace, so her distance would describe the pair, not her own choices.
These decisions also explain why slide 35 treats distance as a description of locomotion rather than a direct score of welfare.
refs: Glaeser SS, Shepherdson D, Lewis K, Prado N, Brown JL, Lee B, Wielebnowski N (2021). Supporting Zoo Asian Elephant (Elephas maximus) Welfare and Herd Dynamics with a More Complex and Expanded Habitat. Animals 11: 2566. https://doi.org/10.3390/ani11092566

Holdgate MR, Meehan CL, Hogan JN, Miller LJ, Soltis J, Andrews J, Shepherdson DJ (2016). Walking Behavior of Zoo Elephants: Associations between GPS-Measured Daily Walking Distances and Environmental Factors, Social Factors, and Welfare Indicators. PLOS ONE 11: e0150331. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0150331

new_slides.title: A temporary hormone rise can signal healthy coping
body: Glucocorticoids mobilize energy and adjust physiology when demands increase, and they rise in response to positive challenges such as exploration and social excitement as well as threats. A healthy stress response rises with a challenge and then returns toward baseline; **chronic stress** is a sustained elevation that no longer subsides.

Most of the Oregon elephants had their highest and most variable metabolite values during construction, and in the new habitat their values became less variable without a sustained climb. Glaeser and colleagues interpret that sequence as adaptive responses to change followed by acclimation, with no sign of chronic elevation.

Social relationships may have helped. Affiliative contact can buffer the stress response in social species, and the herd showed bouts of affiliation directed at aroused members, consistent with the stable bonds described for this group.

figure.caption: Glaeser et al. (2021), Fig. 5(a–d). Individual glucocorticoid metabolite concentrations across habitat phases.

transcript: Slides 28 and 29 present each elephant's metabolite concentrations across habitat phases; the function of glucocorticoids determines whether the construction peak is a warning or a normal response.
Glucocorticoids serve a function, not only a warning.

Glaeser and colleagues point out that the stimuli that activate the stress response can be positive or negative, which is why they paired hormone data with reproductive, behavioral and health measures.
All females kept cycling normally through construction, an independent sign that the hormonal changes did not disrupt reproductive physiology.
The shape of the record distinguishes acute from chronic.
A rise in variability during construction means some samples were very high while others were ordinary, the pattern expected from repeated short responses to new events.
The decline of both median and variability in the new habitat is the evidence against chronic stress; a sustained plateau would have suggested the opposite.
Companions can buffer a response.
The authors cite evidence that affiliative interaction with conspecifics buffers the stress response and report affiliative bouts directed at aroused herdmates.
This connects the endocrine record to the predominantly friendly social repertoire on slide 33, while remaining a proposed explanation rather than a tested one.
refs: Glaeser SS, Shepherdson D, Lewis K, Prado N, Brown JL, Lee B, Wielebnowski N (2021). Supporting Zoo Asian Elephant (Elephas maximus) Welfare and Herd Dynamics with a More Complex and Expanded Habitat. Animals 11: 2566. https://doi.org/10.3390/ani11092566

new_slides.title: Food that must be found turns walking into foraging
body: Glaeser and colleagues kept total foraging and feeding time nearly constant between habitats, yet time spent working at food-delivery devices rose about six-fold, from 3.8% to 24.5% of observations. The change was in how food was obtained, not how much time went to eating.

Dispersed timed feeders and unpredictable delivery make travel part of getting food, which engages the appetitive phase that a fixed ration skips. This fits the view the authors cite that elephant walking is largely appetitive: elephants walk to reach resources, so walking rises when resources must be sought.

The transition also varied by individual. One female spent her first weeks waiting near gates for keepers, apparently expecting food to be delivered, and switched to the feeders later than her herdmates, while the calf adopted them readily.

figure.caption: Glaeser et al. (2021), Fig. 10. Interactions with food resources, enrichment objects and habitat features.

new_slides.cite: Glaeser et al. (2021); Holdgate et al. (2016)
transcript: Slides 25, 26 and 34 report more walking and more engagement with food-delivery resources; the motivational structure of foraging connects these results to each other and to the pacing findings on slide 5.
The redistribution was within feeding, not added to it.
Foraging and feeding together occupied 36.6% of observations in the old habitat and 39.9% in the new one, close to the same share of the day.
Feeding without a device fell by about half while feeding from devices rose, so the elephants worked for a larger share of what they ate.
Walking follows resources.
Holdgate and colleagues found longer walking with more diverse and less predictable feeding, and suggested that dynamic feeding promotes exploration.
Glaeser and colleagues observed elephants checking feeders as they moved through the habitat, which is the behavioral link between food distribution and distance.
Learned expectations slow the switch.
A female that had long received food from keepers waited at the gates for deliveries, and keepers calling her to the feeders may have unintentionally prolonged the transition.
The calf, with the shortest history of keeper feeding, was usually first into new areas and learned the diverse feeders quickly.
refs: Glaeser SS, Shepherdson D, Lewis K, Prado N, Brown JL, Lee B, Wielebnowski N (2021). Supporting Zoo Asian Elephant (Elephas maximus) Welfare and Herd Dynamics with a More Complex and Expanded Habitat. Animals 11: 2566. https://doi.org/10.3390/ani11092566

Holdgate MR, Meehan CL, Hogan JN, Miller LJ, Soltis J, Andrews J, Shepherdson DJ (2016). Walking Behavior of Zoo Elephants: Associations between GPS-Measured Daily Walking Distances and Environmental Factors, Social Factors, and Welfare Indicators. PLOS ONE 11: e0150331. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0150331

new_slides.title: Deep water serves a drive that food does not satisfy
body: Wild king penguins hunt lantern fish at average depths of 120 to 150 m. The old pool was 2 m deep; the new one, about 8 m. Given depth, the birds spent most of their underwater time between 2 and 4 m and little below 6 m, so the extra depth was used but the pool floor held little attraction.

Zoo penguins receive their fish by hand or in pans, so swimming is not required for feeding. Fuller and colleagues found that swimming nevertheless followed the wild seasonal pattern, highest outside breeding and lowest around molt, and they interpret it as an intrinsic drive.

On land, walking fell as swimming rose, and overall activity stayed about the same while its venue shifted to water. Habitat design therefore redirected a fixed motivation to be active rather than creating more activity.

figure.caption: Fuller et al. (2023), Fig. 4. Time spent in different water-depth categories.

transcript: Slides 36 to 39 report more swimming and deeper swimming in the new king-penguin habitat; the species' natural diving behavior and the seasonal timing of swimming explain what that change means for the birds.
The comparison point is a deep-diving forager.
Time-depth recorders on wild king penguins established their foraging depths, the same kind of instrument used in this zoo study.
The zoo pools could never match those depths, so the relevant finding is the shift away from the surface once depth became available, together with avoidance of the bottom.
Seasonal timing points to an internal drive.
Swimming rose and fell across the breeding cycle and molt in the same order seen in wild birds, even though food arrived the same way all year.
Swimming that tracks the animal's own annual cycle rather than the feeding schedule is the evidence the authors use for intrinsic motivation.
Activity was redistributed, not increased.
In the old habitat the penguins often walked in a line around the perimeter of the circular land area, a pattern much less pronounced in the larger habitat.
Elephants show a related lesson on slide 35: the amount of movement is a weaker indicator than the kind of movement and the motivation it serves.
refs: Fuller G, Jones M, Gartland KN, Zalewski S, Heintz MR, Allard S (2023). The Benefits of Increased Space and Habitat Complexity for the Welfare of Zoo-Housed King Penguins (Aptenodytes patagonicus). Animals 13: 2312. https://doi.org/10.3390/ani13142312

extra_figures.caption: Fuller et al. (2023), Fig. 2. A king penguin wearing a flipper-mounted time–depth recorder.

new_slides.title: Crowding raises aggression where penguins compete for space
body: In wild king penguin colonies, aggression depends mainly on breeding stage and on position: central sites are preferred, and birds in the crowded center fight to defend them. Aggression in a zoo flock is therefore expected to rise with breeding and with crowding.

Fuller and colleagues found the most agonistic behavior during the breeding season in both habitats, matching the wild pattern, and more aggression in the old habitat in both study phases. Keepers had even opened an extra area during breeding in the old building to reduce fighting, and aggression stayed higher there anyway.

Visibility complicates other social measures. The birds courted in a sheltered area of the new habitat that observers could not see, so increases in positive behavior partly depend on what was visible, whereas the aggression difference persisted despite this bias.

figure.caption: Fuller et al. (2023), Fig. 5. Behavioral time budgets in the two habitats.

transcript: Slides 40 and 41 report changes in proximity, positive behavior and aggression in the king penguins; wild colony behavior and the study's observational limits explain how strongly each change can be attributed to space.
Space is a contested resource in a colony.
Fuller and colleagues report that territory location is, besides breeding stage, the main predictor of aggression in wild king penguins, with fights concentrated in crowded colony centers.
In a smaller habitat more birds share each preferred spot, so the same breeding motivation produces more encounters that end in conflict.
Mitigation in the old habitat strengthens the conclusion.
Opening extra space during breeding should have reduced the old-habitat aggression, so its remaining excess is conservative evidence for a design effect.
The authors therefore attribute the aggression difference to social density related to habitat design.
Observed rates depend on what observers can see.
The sheltered courting area, called lover's lane by keepers, hid many social interactions in the new habitat during one phase.
Elephant displacement on slide 22 and penguin spacing on slide 40 make the same point from another angle: room to move apart can replace conflict with spacing.

new_slides.title: Population risk factors point to causes but cannot prove them
body: **Epidemiology** studies how outcomes are distributed across a population in order to identify risk factors. Greco and colleagues observed 89 elephants at 39 zoos and estimated each factor's association with stereotypy while holding the others in the model constant, so time housed alone and number of transfers were assessed alongside species, age and sex.

Holding other factors constant removes some confounds, but direction remains unresolved. Transfers could produce stereotypy by disrupting relationships, or elephants that already showed stereotypy might be moved more often, and an observational survey cannot tell these apart.

The strength of the approach is breadth. A single-zoo study like Harvey and colleagues' traces individual relationships in detail but cannot say whether its pattern is general; a population study finds general patterns that individual studies can then test.

figure.caption: Glaeser et al. (2021), Fig. 6(a–f). Individual and combined elephant activity budgets.

new_slides.cite: Greco et al. (2016); Harvey et al. (2018)
transcript: Slides 42 and 43 report risk factors for elephant stereotypy from a multi-zoo survey; the logic of epidemiological models explains what those associations can establish.
Multi-variable models separate overlapping factors.
Greco and colleagues tested dozens of social, housing, management and life-history variables and kept those that predicted stereotypy when considered together.
Their reported effects are conditional on the other variables, which is why Asian species membership, time housed alone, time with juveniles and transfers appear as separate contributions.
Association leaves direction open.
The authors frame transfers and the death of herdmates as disruptions of social relationships, a plausible causal route.

The same association would arise if stereotypic elephants were more likely to be moved, so the finding identifies a risk factor to be tested rather than an established cause, the same caution slide 23 applies to relatedness.
Broad and detailed designs complement each other.
Holdgate and colleagues used the same population approach for walking on slide 35, which is how they could establish that distance did not predict foot, joint or body-condition outcomes.
Detailed individual records, such as the activity budgets on slide 30, show how a factor plays out in particular animals.
